newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street stocks weighed down by Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street stocks weighed down by Greenspan.

text.p: Stocks fell Wednesday after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan rattled Wall Street by questioning the sustainability of the market's powerful rally.

At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was off 89.66 points at 6,948.55, although it recovered from a loss of more than 100 points. As recently as Tuesday of last week, the index romped to a record close of 7,067.46.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances by 16-7 on volume of about 337 million shares.
The Nasdaq Composite index was off 8.01 points to 1,339.68. The American Stock Exchange index lost 3.80 to 596.19.
The bond market also fell, with the 30-year Treasury bond down nearly 1-1/2 points, and its yield jumping to 6.77 percent from Tuesday's close of 6.66 percent.
In his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress, Greenspan delivered an upbeat assessment of the economy but voiced concern about soaring stock prices and the risk of higher inflation.
He warned that financial markets, including investors in stocks and junk bonds, might be over-optimistic about the economic outlook and urged caution.

"I was a bit surprised that he made the stock market such a priority in his testimony," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "He really went out of his way to talk the market down.
"I knew he would say something about it, but not to this extent. Those are the comments that clobbered us earlier. No doubt about it."

In his Congressional speech, the Fed chief said, "Such caution seems especially warranted with regard to the sharp rise in equity prices during the past two years. These gains obviously raise questions of sustainability."
Greenspan also said the Fed might have to raise interest rates in anticipation of inflation rather than waiting until prices actually worsen.

"I'm surprised that we are not down 200 points in the Dow after the chairman of the Federal Reserve said he was not shy about wanting an upward move in rates," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities.
"What should we do now that the man says that profits are overstated, stocks are too high and there might be a pre-emptive strike against inflation? We may be down even more by the end of the day."

Among special situations, Philip Morris Cos. defied the Dow's slide and rose 2-1/4 points to 135-3/8. Philip Morris said Wednesday its directors approved a three-for-one split of the company's common stock, announced a new 3-year $8 billion stock repurchase programme and declared an unchanged quarterly dividend of $1.20 per share on the pre-split common stock.
Dell Computer Corp., the most actively traded Nasdaq issue, was up 1-7/8 at 74, extending gains on the company's announcement of stronger-than-expected fourth quarter results.
